Fribourg
free-BOOR
n. (the Swiss city-state that stayed Catholic between Bern and Geneva, expelled its Reformed, and buried Peter Canisius)
French Fribourg, German Freiburg, the free town, founded by Berthold IV of Zahringen in 1157 on the Sarine.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Fribourg is the Swiss city that did not reform, and its position made that decision matter far beyond its size. Standing on the language border between German and French and geographically between Bern and Geneva, it had been allied with Bern and Savoy and had a share in the common lordships; when Bern went Reformed in 1528 and Geneva in 1536, Fribourg chose the other side, expelled or silenced the evangelicals among its own burghers, broke with Geneva over the alliance, and became the chief Catholic power of western Switzerland. It joined the Golden League of the Catholic cantons in 1586, received the Jesuits and gave them its college in 1582, and Peter Canisius spent his last seventeen years there, dying in 1597 and being buried in the church of St Michael. Fribourg's choice meant that the Reformed Vaud and Geneva were never territorially continuous with Reformed Bern, and that the Catholic recovery in Savoy had a base. The dictionary enters Fribourg because a Reformed dictionary should be able to describe a city that heard the Reformation plainly, from its nearest neighbours, and said no, without reducing that to ignorance or corruption.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a league as a confederacy; a college as a society for the pursuit of learning; to silence as to put to silence; and a burgher as an inhabitant of a borough.

expand to see more

LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense.

COLLEGE, n. A society of men invested with certain powers, engaged in some common pursuit, chiefly of learning.

SILENCE, v. To still; to put to silence; to restrain from speaking or preaching; to prohibit.

BURGHER, n. An inhabitant of a borough or walled town; one who possesses a municipal right.

BORDER, n. The outer edge of anything; the exterior limit of a country or region; a frontier.

Modern Corruption

Swiss city-state between Bern and Geneva which refused the Reformation, expelled its evangelicals, joined the Golden League in 1586, and buried Peter Canisius in 1597.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the assumption that a people who refuse the gospel have not heard it. Fribourg heard it as clearly as any city in Europe, from Bern across the river and Geneva down the lake, with its own burghers preaching it in the 1520s, and the council chose the mass, the alliance with Savoy and eventually the Jesuits. The dictionary holds the choice to have been gravely wrong and declines to explain it away. Scripture shows the same division under the plainest preaching there has ever been: “some believed the things which were spoken, and some believed not” (Act 28:24).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that unbelief under clear preaching is a moral act, not an information problem. Of the Lord's own hearers it is written that “though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him” (Joh 12:37), and of his own disciples that “many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (Joh 6:66). The Athenians' response is the ordinary one and was Fribourg's: “some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter” (Act 17:32).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek apistia rendered unbelief, Greek pisteuo (G4100), to believe; Greek chleuazo (G5512), to mock.

expand to see more

Greek pisteuo (G4100) — to believe, to put trust in; “some believed the things which were spoken, and some believed not”, Acts 28:24.

Greek chleuazo (G5512) — to jeer, to mock; “some mocked”, Acts 17:32.

Greek semeion (G4592) — a sign, a miracle; “though he had done so many miracles before them”, John 12:37.

Greek aperchomai (G565) — to go away, to depart; “many of his disciples went back”, John 6:66.

Greek peripateo (G4043) — to walk, to conduct one's life; “and walked no more with him”, John 6:66.

Usage

"“some believed the things which were spoken, and some believed not” (Act 28:24) — evangelical burghers silenced in the 1520s."

"“though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him” (Joh 12:37) — the Reformation heard from across the river."

"“some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter” (Act 17:32) — the Jesuit college given in 1582."
